![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14268429/assets/6737c9597df5b28719a9b38f9bbefae03d9624e6d94b574a410a57000a48b562.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{2}+C),$ where $C$ is a constant. Given that $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2},$ what is the value of $C?$
question.worked_solution:
The parameter $C$ represents a horizontal shift of the function.

First, we rewrite the function by factoring the horizontal stretch factor, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{2}+C) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{2}(x+\frac{2C}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $x+\frac{2C}{3}$ indicates that the graph of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{2}(x+\frac{2C}{3}))$ is a horizontal translation of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{2}).$ Comparing the two graphs below allows us to determine the amount of this shift.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14268429/assets/6438f318c33223abe9f3d2102e6f9f35bf2a8a6e887955ec9230d22e8294536a.png)

From the diagram, we see that our curve has been obtained by shifting $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3x}{2})$ by $\frac{\pi }{4}-0=\frac{\pi }{4}$ units to the right. Therefore

$$
\frac{2C}{3}=-\frac{\pi }{4}\,⟹\,C=-\frac{3\pi }{8}.
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{2}<C<\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $-\frac{3\pi }{8}$ is in this interval, the value of $C$ is $-\frac{3\pi }{8}.$
